Crow-Armstrong's barrel rate is 13.6% and his hard-hit rate is 48.7%, yet his average exit velocity at 90.6 mph lands only 77th percentile, meaning he's getting to his power through shot selection and contact shape rather than raw brute force, which is exactly why the projection carries 46 home runs against a .280 AVG with 41 stolen bases at 29.5 ft/s sprint speed. If pitchers find a consistent way to exploit that aggressiveness the whole thing compresses, and if they can't, he's a legitimate MVP-conversation outfielder.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-two projected home runs from a 23-year-old third baseman is the headline, but the Statcast profile is what makes it believable: 92.6 mph average exit velocity and a 49.2% hard-hit rate both sit in the 91st-94th percentile range, and an .xwOBA of .360 says the contact quality is already there in real time. The discipline picture is quietly good too, an 11.4% walk rate against a K% of 18.3 that tracks like a hitter who knows the zone, not one who just sells out for power. The whole profile hinges on whether the plate discipline holds as pitchers adjust and attack him harder, because a chase rate that grades below average would be the one lever that brings this ceiling down fast.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz

The problem is a 27.3% strikeout rate that lands near the bottom of the league, and until the whiff rate comes down from 28.1%, there's a ceiling tax on what that raw power can produce across a full season. reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA splits alone frame what he is: .400 as a hitter, .257 as a pitcher, two profiles that would headline separate careers. On the mound, a 2.74 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate pair with a 98.1 mph fastball; at the plate, a 16.0% barrel rate and 93.3 mph average exit velocity back a .381 OBP built on a 13.5% walk rate doing as much work as the raw power. The one thing keeping the hitting profile from being clean is a 31.4% whiff rate that sits in the bottom tier of the game, meaning the .277 projection requires pitchers to keep making mistakes he can punish rather than attacking his swing-and-miss zone consistently. If the elbow holds and both roles stay on the table, this is the most valuable player in baseball; if pitching goes away, what remains is still a .902 OPS DH with 31 projected home runs and legitimate speed.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .472 and the barrel rate at 12.6%, both in the 85th percentile, which is the real story here — this is a plus-power profile that the .799 OPS projection treats conservatively. Stewart's chase and whiff rates land in the bottom third of the league, so the question isn't whether he hits the ball hard enough but whether pitchers eventually exploit those tendencies and drag that .266 projected average toward something uglier. If the contact holds, you're looking at a genuine middle-of-the-order corner bat with 33 projected home runs and enough sneaky speed, 15 projected steals, to keep defenses honest. If the swing decisions erode, the power stays but the average craters, and he becomes a platoon-dependent slugger at first base rather than the everyday corner bat Cincinnati would prefer.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .300 at the 100th percentile, and that's before you account for 30.1 ft/s sprint speed that turns outs into hits at a rate almost no one else can replicate. The Statcast contact profile, xwOBA at .378 and xSLG at .504, both in the 96th percentile, describes a hitter whose actual production has been running below what the ball-in-play data says he deserves, which is why ValuCast's projection lands at .282/.361/.444 with 44 stolen bases across 636 plate appearances. The one real tension is the 33.8% chase rate, a bottom-quarter figure that caps the ceiling if pitchers ever consistently exploit it; if they do, the strikeout rate climbs off its current 17.2% and the walk rate softens from 10.7%, and the offensive case gets harder to make. But the speed, the contact quality, and a projected xSLG of .504 already embedded in the current Statcast read make him the kind of player who finds ways to hurt you before you've finished counting the damage.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The .489 xSLG is what makes this profile worth taking seriously, because most 23-year-olds who chase 37.4% of pitches outside the zone don't also barrel the ball 12.4% of the time at 91.6 mph average exit velocity. Merrill gets away with aggressive plate habits because when he does make contact, he does real damage, and the 29.0 ft/s sprint speed adds a stolen-base dimension the projection captures with 27 projected steals alongside 27 home runs. The honest ceiling here is a high-value everyday outfielder who hits .252/.301/.440 and contributes across all three outcome columns, and if the chase rate climbs further or pitchers learn to exploit it, the .301 OBP leaves almost no margin before the profile starts to erode.

reports.name: James Wood

The contact quality is as loud as it gets, 95.2 mph average exit velocity and 58.6% hard-hit rate both sitting at the very top of the sport, which is why the projection's .385 OBP and .504 SLG feel like conservative translations rather than optimistic ones. reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The .406 OBP across AA & A+ & A is the headline, but 95 walks in 538 plate appearances is what makes it stick. Willits is 18 years old drawing walks at a clip that translates to 12.7 BB%, well above where the average big-league hitter lands, and he's stolen 62 bases this season, so the profile isn't just patience — it moves. The ISO translates to .134, a tick below the MLB mean of .150, so the real dependency is whether the power develops enough that pitchers can't simply pitch around him at the next level. If it does, you're looking at an everyday shortstop; if the power stalls, the walk rate and legs still build a useful player, just not the top-of-the-order anchor the ceiling implies.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The 34-home-run, 34-steal projection is eye-catching, but the Statcast profile tells you exactly how nervous to be about it. His 10.3% barrel rate sits at a genuinely good level, and the .436 xSLG explains why the power translates when he squares it up. The problem is a 36.5% chase rate that lands in the 15th percentile, which feeds a 29.5% whiff rate and ultimately caps how much of that raw punch shows up in actual production. Everything here hinges on whether he can cut the chase rate enough to let the barrel tool breathe, because right now the swing decisions are the ceiling, not the athleticism: his 28.4 ft/s sprint speed is legitimate and the stolen-base projection follows logically from it. If the plate discipline firms up, he's a multi-category shortstop playing at the top of a lineup; if it doesn't, the .838 OPS projection deflates and you're left with real pop and enough swing-and-miss to keep him from reaching it consistently.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics pull in completely opposite directions, and that tension is the whole Walker profile. His 92.6 mph average exit velocity and 49.5% hard-hit rate say the raw thump is genuine, but a 36.0% chase rate and 32.0% whiff rate are what happens when a bat that loud hasn't learned to pick its spots. The xSLG sits at .463 while the xBA trails at .265, which is the Statcast version of the same argument: when he connects, it goes, and the projection's 29 home runs in 671 plate appearances tracks with that shape. If the chase rate comes down, you get an everyday middle-of-the-order corner outfielder; if it stays where it is, you get a big-power bat who costs you in enough other ways to keep him from reaching that ceiling.

reports.name: Josh Naylor
reports.published_report: The 30 stolen bases in the projection are the number that doesn't fit, and the Statcast profile explains why. Naylor makes contact at an elite clip, a 12.3% strikeout rate in the 94th percentile, but he's running on a 24.3 ft/s sprint speed that sits at the 1st percentile, so those steals either come from volume and aggressive managing or they don't come at all. The contact quality is genuinely modest, 87.1 mph average exit velocity and a 4.6% barrel rate both below the 20th percentile, and his xBA of .271 outpacing an xSLG of .383 says he's a bat-to-ball guy whose value lives in contact, not thump. If the strikeout suppression holds and the stolen base total corrects toward what his speed actually supports, what's left is a useful but limited first baseman, a second-division regular whose floor is a good bench bat and whose ceiling rises only if the contact finds more gaps than his exit velocity suggests it should.

reports.name: Brooks Lee
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is pulling in opposite directions, and that tension is what makes Brooks Lee hard to value. His 16.2% strikeout rate is genuinely elite contact quality — the bat doesn't miss, it just doesn't hit the ball hard when it connects, with an 88.1 mph average exit velocity and a 4.2% barrel rate that both sit well below average. The .279 xwOBA is the number that settles the argument: a hitter who makes this much contact but generates this little power and walks at 6.0% ends up as a below-average offensive contributor, and the projection (.255/.303/.432) reflects that honestly. He can play short or third, and the fielding grades decently, so the floor is a useful regular, but he's essentially betting that 25 home runs from below-average contact quality holds, and the underlying shape doesn't make that easy to trust.

Zazueta has walked 20 batters across 103.7 innings at AA & A+, a 1.7 BB/9 that translates to a 2.4 MLB equivalent, well below the league-average 3.2. The strikeout rate holds up too, with 144 punchouts producing a 30% K-BB% that would sit comfortably clear of the 13.5% MLB-average translation. Everything hinges on whether the stuff plays against better bats, because a back-end starter ceiling isn't a criticism, it's the outcome if the profile holds, and a multi-inning relief role is what's left if it doesn't carry past AAA.

reports.name: Angel Martínez
reports.published_report: That 3.0% walk rate is the whole read. The xwOBA sits at .306, which is a bottom-third outcome for a hitter making contact at a .257 xBA clip, and it lands there almost entirely because Martínez chases 42.6% of pitches outside the zone, a rate that slots in at the 3rd percentile. The contact quality is honest — a 20.8% whiff rate and mid-pack barrel numbers suggest he's not flailing when he swings, just swinging at everything pitchers want him to. The projection's .293 OBP on 409 PA is what you get when a hitter has enough bat to stay on a roster but not enough discipline to force pitchers to respect him, and if the chase rate hardens into a career trait rather than a developmental phase, this profile settles as a second-division regular at best, useful against soft stuff but easy to gameplan for any staff with a full scouting report.

reports.name: Jakob Marsee
reports.published_report: The .310 xwOBA sits well below league average, but that's almost beside the point here. This profile is built on a 12.7% walk rate and a 22.3% chase rate, two of the better discipline numbers you'll see, and the bat itself is nowhere close to carrying that patience. An 87.3 mph average exit velo with a 3.6% barrel rate and .328 xSLG means contact is soft and power is limited; the projection's .229/.346/.356 line captures exactly that tension, a guy who gets on base at a useful clip but can't do much damage when he does. The 24 projected steals add genuine leverage, and the 94th-percentile fielding grade gives him a defensive floor that keeps him on a roster, but what this profile hinges on is whether the discipline holds at volume — if pitchers find a consistent approach against him and that walk rate erodes, there's not enough bat or power to compensate, and he slides from low-end regular to high-end bench piece.

reports.name: Lazaro Montes
reports.published_report: Thirty-eight home runs across AAA & AA at age 21, with a .309 ISO that translates to .215 at the MLB level — the power here is loud enough to survive the conversion. The problem is the strikeout rate, which goes from 31% in the minors to a translated 31.1% at the MLB level, well above what the average big-league hitter runs at 22.0%, and that gap is where this profile either justifies a corner-outfield job or shrinks into a matchup piece. Seventy-nine walks across AAA & AA in 542 plate appearances translate to an 11.8% walk rate, clear of the MLB mean of 8.5%, so the floor doesn't collapse even if the contact stays thin. If the swing-and-miss doesn't tighten, he's a bench bat with real power; if it does, there's a second-division regular in here.

reports.name: Munetaka Murakami
reports.published_report: The tension is right there in the Statcast card: a 19.0% barrel rate and 93.7 mph average exit velocity sitting alongside a 42.5% whiff rate and a 35.5% strikeout rate. He makes brutal, barreled contact when he connects, but he connects less often than almost anyone in the league. The .200 xBA tells that story cleanly — the raw power grades out at the very top of the sport, and the ability to lay off chases (22.2%) suggests the zone recognition is genuinely good, which makes the whiff rate inside the zone the real problem. If pitchers keep attacking him with spin and he can't close that gap, a .204/.347/.468 projection line is close to the ceiling rather than a floor, and 34 home runs with a .200 average is a polarizing but real outcome that most lineup constructions can absorb at first base.

reports.name: Nelson Rada
reports.published_report: The .376 OBP at AAA is the whole argument, and it has a hollow center. Rada put up 72 walks against 109 strikeouts across 585 AAA plate appearances in 2026, and the discipline carries over — his MLB-equivalent walk rate comes out to 10.6%, with a strikeout rate that would sit below the MLB mean. That's a useful profile at the top of a lineup. The .085 ISO at AAA translates to .089 at the MLB level, well short of the MLB average, and 43 stolen bases can cover the gap in the minors longer than they can in the majors. If the speed plays and the on-base rate holds, he's a bench or platoon piece in center; if a big-league defense shades him and the power never develops, the hit tool and the legs are what remain.

reports.name: Chase Meidroth
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is bottom-quartile across the board, 87.3 mph average exit velocity, 4.7% barrel rate, .346 xSLG, but the projection still lands at .274/.349/.412 with 16 home runs over 656 plate appearances, and the reason that math works is the 96th-percentile fielding (OAA) paired with a walk rate that keeps his on-base viable. He makes enough contact to stay in lineups, posting a 19.6% whiff rate that ranks in the 79th percentile, and his discipline isn't just avoiding strikeouts: 9.6% walks give him a floor that pure contact hitters at his exit-velo tier don't have. The whole profile hinges on the glove staying elite; if the OAA drifts toward league average, there isn't enough thump in the bat to compensate and he becomes a fringe regular rather than a useful one. Right now, with the defense doing heavy lifting, a second-division everyday infielder is the honest ceiling and the floor isn't far below it.

reports.name: Matt Olson
reports.published_report: Forty-two home runs projected across 704 plate appearances, and the Statcast profile says that number isn't running ahead of itself: a 14.5% barrel rate and 51.8% hard-hit rate both sit in the 94th percentile, with an xSLG of .507 that matches the projected .507 SLG almost exactly. The one internal tension is the strikeout rate, 24.7%, which ranks in just the 27th percentile, and if pitchers find a consistent way to exploit the 25.5% whiff rate, the .253 AVG projection has room to slip. What you're buying is a true power bat who converts contact into damage at an elite rate, not a high-average guy who happens to go deep a lot. The profile holds as long as the exit quality holds, and at 92.4 mph average exit velocity, that's been a durable trait.

reports.name: Heriberto Hernández
reports.published_report: The gap between an .469 xSLG and a 32.5% whiff rate is the whole profile in two numbers. Hernández makes elite contact when he gets to the ball, with a 12.6% barrel rate and 91.2 mph average exit velocity that sit in the 84th and 85th percentiles, but he misses too often to let that power show up cleanly in his batting average — .244 xBA against .469 xSLG is a significant spread. The 23.5% chase rate is genuinely disciplined, which is how he maintains a 10.6% walk rate, so the profile isn't a free-swinger who stumbled into good contact; contact quality and chase avoidance are both real, but the whiff rate on pitches he does swing at is the leak the projection can't paper over. If he tightens the zone-swing contact rate, the projection's .431 SLG with 25 home runs looks conservative; if it stays near 32.5%, the .225 average is probably the ceiling, not the floor, and he becomes a lower-end regular who earns his lineup spot on power and walks alone.

Across AAA, AA, and A this season, Hernandez has 96 strikeouts in 74.7 innings, an 11.6 K/9 that translates to 9.3 at the MLB level, but the 6.4 BB/9 translates to 5.5, nearly double what a typical big-league arm gives away. That gap is the whole profile: the stuff misses bats, but a 53rd-percentile K-BB% says the strikeouts aren't outrunning the control problem by nearly enough. If the walk rate doesn't tighten, you're looking at a reliever or depth piece; if it does, there's a back-end starter in there somewhere, but the evidence strength is rated low and the sample doesn't yet say which way this tips.

reports.name: Wyatt Sanford
reports.published_report: The numbers are loud and the ceiling is quiet. Wyatt Sanford is hitting .282/.417/.546 across A+ & A with 19 home runs and 33 stolen bases in 363 plate appearances, a profile that ranks at the 98th percentile in OPS and 96th in both ISO and slugging against his peer hitter pool. The translation to MLB is where the argument gets complicated: that 31% strikeout rate renders to roughly 32.6% against a league that averages 22.0%, and even with the walk rate translating to a useful 10.6%, that's a contact floor that has swallowed plenty of loud minor-league lines. If the strikeout rate doesn't compress significantly as pitching quality rises, the power and speed become assets on a bench bat rather than an everyday shortstop.

reports.name: Justin Gonzales
reports.published_report: The .385 OBP across AA & A+ at 19 years old is the number that makes you look twice. Gonzales has drawn 68 walks against 101 strikeouts in 507 plate appearances, a discipline profile that translates to a 10.4% walk rate at the MLB level, comfortably ahead of where most hitters sit. The power is the catch: his .183 ISO across AA & A+ softens to a translated .133, and the gap between that figure and the MLB average of .150 is wide enough that the ceiling hinges entirely on whether the raw pop develops rather than gets squeezed out by better arms. reports.name: Noah Cameron
reports.published_report: The 3.92 ERA projection looks better than the underlying Statcast work deserves. His xERA sits at 4.06 with an xwOBA of .310, both right at the median for MLB starters, and his 21.6% strikeout rate ranks below average, which means he's pitching to contact more than he's winning the at-bat. What keeps him viable is a 7.5% walk rate that grades out well above league average and a 26.3% whiff rate with 2310 rpm on his fastball spin — not a swing-and-miss arsenal, but enough deception to make the low-velocity (92.5 mph) fastball play. The whole profile hinges on limiting barrels; his 8.2% barrel rate is already above the comfortable range, and if hitters start squaring him up more often, a fourth-rotation slot becomes fifth real fast.

reports.name: Brandon Marsh

reports.name: Garrett Mitchell
reports.published_report: The exit velocity is a 97th-percentile number, 93.2 mph average, sitting beside a 35.9% whiff rate that ranks in the 2nd percentile. That is the whole Mitchell problem in two figures. When he makes contact, the ball genuinely goes: 52.6% hard-hit rate, a 22.7% chase rate that says he isn't chasing himself into those whiffs, which means the swing-and-miss is happening in the zone, and that's the harder fix. The projection at .262/.353/.419 across 532 PA is probably the ceiling of what you get if the strikeouts stay stuck at 31.5%, because the 11.3% walk rate and elite speed at 29.8 ft/s keep him afloat as an on-base and baserunning contributor even when the bat misses. If the contact rate ever moves even a little, the exit velo profile turns him into something more interesting; if it doesn't, he's a bench outfielder with genuine tools and a concrete ceiling.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the most interesting thing in this profile, and it might also be the most misleading part. At A+ across 486 plate appearances, Flewelling has drawn 71 walks against 132 strikeouts, a 15% walk rate that translates to roughly 11% at the MLB level, a figure meaningfully ahead of where MLB hitters sit on average, but his 27% strikeout rate at A+ becomes something closer to 30.5% when you run it through the level adjustment, and that's a hard number to build a catcher's career around. The .208 ISO at A+ is loud for a 19-year-old at that level, yet it softens to about .144 in MLB-equivalent terms, which lands right at the league-average power band, meaning the profile that looks like a power-and-patience bat in High-A looks more like a fringe regular once you translate it. Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

reports.name: Evan Carter

His xwOBA sits at .277 and his xBA at .201, both near the absolute floor of the league, and the exit velocity numbers, 87.6 mph average and 34.8% hard-hit rate, confirm he's not squaring the ball up with any regularity. Across 61.7 innings at A+, he's punched out 73 hitters at 10.7 K/9, but 51 walks at 7.4 BB/9 have produced a 1.8 WHIP and a 6.70 ERA that leaves almost no argument for the present. Translate that profile to MLB-equivalent and the strikeouts land near league average while the walk rate lands at 6.4, roughly double what big-league starters typically allow, and a K-BB% of 8.6% against the 13.5% norm tells you exactly how much the free passes are eating the upside. The entire profile hinges on whether the walks compress as he matures, because if they don't, the strikeout ceiling has nowhere to go and he's a depth arm by ceiling and floor.

reports.name: Chad Patrick
reports.published_report: The 10.4% walk rate is the thing you keep coming back to. Patrick's contact profile is genuinely solid, a 6.2% barrel rate and 36.7% hard-hit rate that say hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact, and his 26.4% whiff rate adds to the picture. But a walk rate sitting in the 24th percentile poisons the well, because a guy who can't locate consistently enough to stay ahead in counts is one bad stretch from watching a tidy contact profile unravel. The projection's 3.13 ERA against a 4.12 xERA is the gap you need to explain, and the walks are most of the explanation: useful multi-inning arm for Milwaukee right now, something more if the command ever firms up.

reports.name: AJ Blubaugh
reports.published_report: The 10.6% walk rate is the number that defines him, and it defines him badly. Blubaugh generates whiffs at a decent clip, 28.2% Whiff%, and his 95.8 mph fastball gives him a genuine weapon, but hitters don't need to chase him because he finds the zone on his own terms often enough — his 28.7% Chase% sits near the bottom quarter of the league. The barrel rate at 10.1% is the other weight on the scale: he gets swings and misses in the zone, then surrenders hard contact when hitters do connect, which is exactly why the xERA of 4.23 tells a different story than a 3.6 ERA projection. If the walk rate tightens, there's a useful middle-relief arm here; if it doesn't, he's a high-leverage matchup guy who becomes a liability the moment a lineup stops swinging at borderline pitches.

Across 414 plate appearances at AA in 2026, Will Turner is hitting .193 with a .219 BABIP, and the only reason he's still worth watching is that he's drawn 84 walks, a 20% BB% that translates to 14.8% against a major-league environment where most hitters sit at 8.5%. The power has shape: 18 home runs and a .224 ISO at AA, translating to .164 at the MLB level, but the .193 average isn't a cold-streak waiting to correct — that BABIP says the contact quality is genuinely thin. If the walk rate holds in the upper minors and the ISO travels, there's a low-end regular in the margins; if pitchers decide he'll take the strike, what's left is a bench piece.

reports.name: Robby Snelling

The surface numbers are loud: 44 strikeouts against 15 walks in those 29 innings translates to a K-BB% that sits at the 98th percentile of the pitcher pool, and the MLB-equivalent read puts his K/9 at 9.9 while the league translates to 8.6. The problem is that six starts is a thin thread to hang a rotation future on, and the 60-day move means whatever health question ended his season hasn't been answered yet. If he comes back right, there's a real arm here; if he doesn't, the floor is bullpen depth and not much more.

reports.name: Blake Wehunt
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the best thing about Blake Wehunt, which tells you most of what you need to know. Across AAA & AA this season he's posted a 3.2 BB/9 that translates cleanly to the majors, and the 3.5 ERA over 100.4 innings is tidy enough, but the strikeout side doesn't hold up: 9.3 K/9 in the minors melts to an 8.1 MLB equivalent, and a K-BB% that translates to 12.6% sits just below where big-league starters need to be to avoid living on the margin. He can be useful as long as the command stays where it is; if hitters stop chasing and the walk rate creeps up, there's no strikeout upside to absorb the damage. Depth arm, honest floor, honest ceiling.

reports.name: Ty Southisene
reports.published_report: The contact-and-patience combination is legitimately special; the power is the problem. Across A+ & A this season, Southisene is hitting .300 with a 12% strikeout rate and 47 walks in 368 plate appearances, a plate-discipline profile that translates to roughly a 17.8% K rate and 9.7% walk rate at the MLB level — both sitting comfortably below and above what big-league hitters typically post. The ISO of .080 across A+ & A is the wall everything runs into, and the MLB-equivalent translation lands at .087, less than two-thirds of what the average major leaguer produces for power. The 34 stolen bases add a real dimension, and if the contact and strike-zone feel hold as he climbs, there's a path to a useful table-setter, but without a power signal emerging by Double-A, this profile ends at a bench piece whose value lives entirely in the top of the lineup.

reports.name: Brayan Buelvas
reports.published_report: The .236 ISO across AAA & AA is loud for a 24-year-old center fielder, and the .509 slugging translates to a .176 MLB-equivalent ISO, which clears the mlb average of .15 by enough to matter. The problem is sitting right next to it: 117 strikeouts in 450 plate appearances, and when you run that contact rate through the translation, his K% lands at 26.3% against an MLB average of 22.0%. His walk rate translates almost exactly to league average, so there's no patience cushion absorbing the swing-and-miss. If the power plays and the strikeouts compress even modestly, he's a second-division regular with real thump; if the contact rate holds where it is at the MLB level, the bat becomes too thin for everyday center field and what's left is a bench bat with one carrying tool.

reports.name: Tyler Black
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that exposes its limits. Across 430 plate appearances at AAA, Tyler Black has drawn 64 walks, a 15% clip that translates to a 12.1% MLB-equivalent, well above the 8.5% league baseline, and that discipline is what's keeping a .246/.368/.387 line from looking like what it really is: a guy who can't hit for power. The ISO translates to .125 at the MLB level, below league average, and seven home runs in 430 AAA plate appearances isn't the kind of thump a left fielder needs to force a big-league roster decision. If the walks and a reasonable strikeout rate (23.3% MLB-equivalent, roughly league average) were supporting real power, this would be a different conversation, but the plate discipline is carrying everything, and there's only so far it goes when the slug isn't there.

Floor is a bench bat; if the plate discipline translates cleanly, there's a low-end regular in there.

reports.name: Bryce Cunningham
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the honest problem. Across AA & A+, Cunningham has struck out 96 batters in 105.3 innings, and when that translates to a 7.0 K/9 in MLB context, it sits well below what big-league hitters are used to seeing. The walk numbers are more forgiving: a 3.3 BB/9 at his level lands in the 79th percentile of his pitcher pool, and a 1.3 WHIP suggests he's limiting damage well enough that the 4.6 ERA probably overstates the mess. The translated K-BB% of 10.2% tells the fuller story, running notably short of the MLB average 13.5%, and that gap doesn't leave margin for any command regression at all. Bullpen or depth is the right framing, not because he's failing, but because the ceiling isn't there for him to grow past it as a starter.

The discipline translates well enough: 59 walks against 80 strikeouts at A+ becomes 10.6% walks and 23.4% strikeouts at the MLB level, both directionally fine, with the walk rate sitting above the MLB mean. The power doesn't make the same trip, with an MLB-equivalent ISO of .122 where the typical big leaguer sits closer to .150. If the speed holds and the hit tool keeps the OBP functional, he's a useful bench piece with a real late-inning role; if the bat flattens against upper-minors velocity, the speed alone doesn't carry a corner outfielder's profile.

reports.name: Trevor Cohen
reports.published_report: The calling card is a 12% strikeout rate across AA & A+, and the translation puts him at 16.6% in the majors, comfortably below where most big-league hitters land. Cohen has also swiped 46 bases in 608 plate appearances, which is a real skill even if the power profile doesn't follow — his translated ISO sits at .095 while the MLB average is .150, and the raw .109 across AA & A+ isn't telling a different story. At 22 with plus contact and plus speed, there's a pathway to a useful fourth-outfielder type if he can get on base consistently enough for the stolen-base weapon to matter, but a .370 OBP built on a .335 BABIP at this level deserves some skepticism on the translation. If the contact rate travels and the on-base holds, you have a legitimate defensive center fielder who creates value with his legs; if the BABIP normalizes and the power stays this thin, he's a bench piece whose ceiling is already visible.

reports.name: Mason Peters
reports.published_report: The 2.1 ERA across A+ & A is the loud number, but what makes it worth taking seriously is the shape behind it: 87 strikeouts in 64.3 innings with only 19 walks, a 0.9 WHIP, a K-BB% of 27 that ranks at the 98th percentile in his pool. Strip that down to what it translates to at the MLB level and it deflates quickly — the strikeout rate comes out to 8.4 per nine, essentially matching what an average major-league arm produces, and the walk rate lands in the same neighborhood, so the margins that look dominant in A-ball basically become a league-average pitcher. That's the whole profile: the stuff plays up in the lower minors, and if it doesn't add a genuine swing-and-miss weapon as he climbs, the floor is a depth arm with no real ceiling to argue over.
